html:
The square on top of the Capitoline Hill in Rome, between the Roman Forum and the Campus Martius, laid out by Michelangelo for Pope Paul III. The hill has been the seat of the city's government since the Middle Ages, when the people of Rome took over a fortress built on the ruins of the Tabularium, the ancient record office, and made it the house of their senate. By the 16th century the hilltop was so run down that it was called goat hill. Paul III wanted a symbol of a new Rome to impress the emperor Charles V, who came to the city in 1536, and Michelangelo's first designs date from 1534.

Michelangelo turned the square around, so that it faced St Peter's, the new centre of the city, rather than the old Forum behind it. He gave matching fronts to the two old palaces, the Senators' Palace and the Palace of the Conservators, which stood at an angle of about 80 degrees, and added a third, the Palazzo Nuovo, as a mirror of the second, closing a square shaped like a trapezoid. Their giant pilasters, running through two storeys, were the first used on public buildings. He also designed the double stair of the Senators' Palace, with statues of the river gods of the Tiber and the Nile, the broad ramp of steps called the Cordonata climbing from the street below, and an oval paving with a twelve-pointed star. Work went slowly: Michelangelo saw only the double stair finished, and the rest was built after his death in 1564.

At the centre he set the gilded bronze statue of the emperor Marcus Aurelius on horseback, brought from the square of the Lateran; the original is now indoors and a copy stands outside. The Palace of the Conservators, built in 1453 by Bernardo Rossellino, stands on the platform of the ancient Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus, parts of which can still be seen. Together the palaces hold the Capitoline Museums, counted among the oldest public museums, begun in 1471 when Pope Sixtus IV gave the people of Rome ancient bronzes such as the She-wolf and the colossal head of Constantine.
